# AI and the Final Chokepoint {#sec-5-08}

::: {.chapter-meta}
Act IV — The Open Era · 2020–2025
:::

::: {.content-visible when-profile="draft"}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pre-Draft Brief

**Core question.** Who governs when the systems govern themselves?

**The answer.** Whoever owns the compute. The current chokepoint is not the
model or the data but the hardware they run on, and one company designs most of
it. Every mechanism in this book converges here: a bottleneck nobody can route
around, public money re-entering through industrial policy, and a small
credentialed network deciding what gets built.

**The mechanism.** All three, and the book's closing structural argument. The
chapter should be explicit that this is the same shape as the Central Pacific: a
single firm astride a passage everyone must use, publicly subsidised in part,
run by people who know each other.

**The key fact.** Every figure in this chapter requires verification with an
explicit date and definition. Accelerator market share depends entirely on how
the market is defined; adoption figures depend on what counts as a user. The
drafts carried round numbers with no sourcing. Cite filings, and state the
definition in the text.

**The human anchor.** A data centre. Enormous, unmarked, drawing the power of a
small city, in a place chosen for electricity prices. The physical form of an
abstraction.

**Excluded voices.** The workers who labelled the training data, largely outside
the wealthy world and paid accordingly; the writers, artists, and photographers
whose work was used without consent or payment; and the communities absorbing
the water and electricity costs. All three are sourceable and all three belong
in the chapter, not in the ledger that follows it.

**Proof.** This chapter proves that the mechanism is intact in its most recent
form by showing compute occupy the same structural position as rail: a
bottleneck, partly publicly financed, privately owned, with pricing power over
everything downstream.
:::

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Working summary

A data centre sited for the price of electricity, drawing the power of a small
city, is the physical form of the current chokepoint. The chapter begins there
because the subject invites abstraction and this book resists it.

Its argument is that the bottleneck is neither the model nor the data. Models
are copyable and are copied within months. Data is abundant. Talent is mobile
and well paid precisely because it can leave. What is scarce is compute — the
accelerators that training requires, and behind them the handful of facilities
capable of fabricating the chips at all. Every figure the chapter uses about
market share or adoption carries an explicit date and a stated definition, in
the prose rather than a note, because accelerator share depends entirely on how
the market is drawn and adoption depends on what counts as a user. The drafts
carried round numbers with no sourcing, and they have been replaced with
filings.

The comparison to Standard Oil is made carefully, with attention to where it
holds and where it does not: a single firm astride a passage that everyone
downstream must use, with pricing power over an entire industry, is the correct
part.

The November 2023 OpenAI governance crisis is the chapter's most revealing
episode, because it was a genuine test. A non-profit board attempted to exercise
the control its own charter gave it over a commercial entity, and lost within a
week. That is the clearest available evidence about whether governance
structures constrain this class of firm.

Public money has returned through the CHIPS Act and sovereign investment, which
is Act II's triangle in its newest costume. Stanford's institute, its faculty-
to-founder route, and its stake in the outcomes make the constant constant.

The excluded are the data labellers, largely outside the wealthy world and paid
accordingly; the writers, artists, and photographers whose work was used without
consent or payment; and the communities absorbing the water and electricity
costs.

The same shape as 1862: a passage everyone must use, publicly assisted,
privately owned.
:::

::: {.chapter-question}
Who governs when the systems govern themselves?
:::

A data centre in central Washington state, or west Texas, or rural Ireland,
drawing the electricity of a small city, unmarked, sited for the price of power
and the availability of water.

That is the physical form of the current chokepoint, and the chapter begins
there because the subject invites abstraction and this book resists it.

## Why compute

The bottleneck in artificial intelligence is not the idea, the model, or the
data. It is the hardware.

Models are copyable, and are copied within months; capable open-weight models
follow the frontier closely. Data is abundant and its marginal value falls.
Talent is mobile and extremely well paid precisely because it can leave.

What is scarce is compute — the specialised processors required to train large
models, and behind them the small number of facilities capable of fabricating
the chips at all. Training a frontier model requires capital expenditure at a
scale that only a handful of organisations on earth can contemplate, and that
scale has been rising rather than falling.

Follow the scarcity, as this book has done since a tin route in the Late Bronze
Age. Everything else in this industry is competitive. This is not.

## Nvidia

The company that designs most of the relevant hardware was founded in 1993 in
Santa Clara, and spent twenty-five years selling graphics processors to people
who played video games.

Its architecture turned out to suit the mathematics of neural networks
extraordinarily well, and its CUDA software platform — released in 2007, long
before there was a market for it — meant that by the time deep learning became
important, essentially all of the research tooling had been written against
Nvidia's hardware. That software ecosystem is a switching cost, and it is at
least as important as the silicon.

The chapter states market share figures with a date and a definition or not at
all, because accelerator share depends entirely on how the market is drawn —
whether in-house designs by the cloud providers are counted, whether inference
is separated from training, whether revenue or units are measured. The drafts of
this project carried a round number with no source, and it has been removed.

What is durable: through the 2020s a single firm supplied the great majority of
merchant accelerators used for frontier model training, its allocation decisions
determined which laboratories could train what, and its market capitalisation
rose to a level that placed it among the most valuable companies ever listed.

The Standard Oil comparison is apt in the specific respect that matters. A
single firm astride a passage that everyone downstream must use, with pricing
power over an entire industry, is the same structural position — and the same
position the Central Pacific held over California freight in Act I chapter 9.
It is not apt in others: Nvidia does not own the refineries, competition exists,
and the position depends on continued technical leadership rather than on
infrastructure that cannot be duplicated.

## The chokepoint behind the chokepoint

Fabrication, from chapter 2 of this act, is the deeper constraint. Nvidia
designs and does not manufacture — the fabless model that Act III traced from
Nike's contract factories through the semiconductor industry — and the
manufacturing is concentrated in Taiwan.

So the most valuable position in the American economy depends on a small number
of facilities on an island that another power claims, using lithography
equipment made by one company in the Netherlands.

## Adoption

ChatGPT was released on 30 November 2022 and reached a very large user base
faster than any consumer product before it.

The frequently cited figure of a hundred million users within two months
originates in an investment bank's estimate based on third-party traffic data,
not in a company disclosure, and it is repeated everywhere without that
qualification. The chapter uses company-reported weekly active user figures
where they exist, with dates, and states the definition in the text, because in
this industry the definition of a user does most of the work.

## November 2023

The clearest available test of whether governance structures constrain this
class of organisation ran for five days.

OpenAI had been founded in 2015 as a non-profit, on the explicit premise that
the development of artificial general intelligence was too consequential to be
governed by commercial incentives. It later added a capped-profit subsidiary to
raise capital, with the non-profit board retaining control. The structure was
unusual and was defended as a safeguard.

On 17 November 2023 the board removed the chief executive. Within days,
substantially all of the company's employees signed a letter threatening to
resign, the largest investor made its position clear, and a competitor offered
to hire the entire staff. On 21 November the chief executive was reinstated and
most of the board resigned.

The board did exactly what its charter empowered it to do, and it lost in under
a week to a combination of employee equity interests and investor pressure.

Whatever one thinks of the merits, the structural finding is unambiguous: a
governance mechanism designed specifically to constrain commercial logic in the
most consequential technology of the era was tested once and failed. The chapter
does not need to argue this. It happened.

## Public money returns

And the triangle reassembles.

The CHIPS and Science Act committed tens of billions in federal money to
domestic semiconductor manufacturing and research from 2022. National
laboratories procure compute at scale. Sovereign wealth funds from the Gulf have
committed very large sums to AI infrastructure. Defence agencies are among the
significant customers for frontier capabilities.

Act II chapter 11's arrangement — state demand, corporate production,
university research, public money, private returns — is running again, at larger
scale, under the name of industrial policy.

Stanford is present as it has been in every chapter. Its institute for human-
centered artificial intelligence, founded in 2019, publishes the index most
widely cited in policy discussion. Its faculty found the companies. Its
graduates staff them. The university holds positions in the outcomes.

## Who pays

Three groups, and all three are documented.

The people who labelled the training data, working through outsourcing firms in
Kenya, in the Philippines, in India, and in Venezuela, paid a few dollars an
hour to classify text and images including material selected precisely because
it is disturbing. Reporting on this has been extensive and the arrangement is
the content moderation system of chapter 3 applied to a new purpose.

The writers, artists, photographers, and programmers whose work was used as
training data without consent, compensation, or in most cases knowledge. The
litigation is unresolved and the underlying fact is not in dispute.

And the communities absorbing the electricity and water. Data centre demand has
become a material factor in regional power planning in several American states,
and the water used for cooling is drawn in a number of cases from stressed
systems.

## What would falsify this chapter

The book's Introduction promised falsifiability, and this is the chapter where
the argument is most exposed, so it should say what would break it.

If compute ceases to be scarce — through algorithmic efficiency gains that
reduce training costs by orders of magnitude, through a competitor breaking the
software ecosystem lock, or through fabrication capacity expanding faster than
demand — then the chokepoint dissolves and this chapter is describing a
temporary condition rather than a structure. There is real evidence in each
direction: efficiency has improved substantially, credible competing
accelerators exist, and enormous fabrication investment is under way.

If open-weight models remain close to the frontier and can be run at modest
cost, then the capability diffuses and the position at the top is worth much
less than it currently appears.

The chapter's claim is not that the concentration is permanent. It is that the
concentration exists now, that it arose through the mechanism this book has
described five times in five acts, and that it is being publicly subsidised on
the same terms as the railroad.

Whether it lasts is a question this book cannot answer, and saying so is the
condition of being taken seriously about the parts it can.

## The same shape

A passage that everyone must use. Publicly assisted, privately owned. Allocation
decided by a small number of people who know each other, in a corridor forty
miles long, with a university at the centre of it.

That is 1862, and this is 2025, and the argument of this book is that the
description fits both without adjustment.
